narrative:
The model estimated a 52.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty; it means the available information made failure slightly more likely than passing, and because your law school application was tied to this prediction, it was rejected.

The strongest factor behind that result was your LSAT score. At 21, it is well below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and in the model it was the most influential feature, pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the second most influential feature. Although it is close to the accepted-student average of 3.23, its role in your case leaned toward passing and therefore worked against the failure prediction. Your first-year decile was the third most influential feature; at 8 compared with an accepted-student average of 6, it also leaned toward passing. Those positive signals were not enough to offset the LSAT-driven concern, leaving the estimate just above the midpoint.

To improve your chances, focus first on the LSAT: consider structured preparation and a retake if you can raise your score substantially. Strengthen your application with updated academic evidence, a clear addendum explaining any context, and advice from admissions staff. Consider schools or programs with more flexible admission standards, and ask whether conditional or provisional admission is possible.
